title: The Prank

jokes.text: Larry introduces the Butthole Surfers by saying 'their song is called Ulcer Breakout. This is all about me. My doctor wrote this song.'
jokes.setup: Larry is doing a standard late-night band introduction for the Butthole Surfers, a notoriously transgressive band.
jokes.punchline: He pivots to make it about his own gastric ailments, framing 'Ulcer Breakout' as personally commissioned by his physician.
jokes.explanation: A deft piece of character comedy — Larry's reflexive self-involvement transforms a band introduction into a health complaint. The joke is quick, character-specific, and uses the absurd band name/song title as a springboard. It's the kind of thing only Larry Sanders would do.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Paralegal? I always thought that was a lawyer in a wheelchair.

jokes.text: Larry introduces 'Butthole Surfers' on late-night television, deadpan and formal, treating the name as entirely unremarkable.
jokes.setup: Larry delivers the band name 'Butthole Surfers' in the same polished, professional late-night host register he'd use for any act.
jokes.punchline: The absurdity of the name set against the total normalcy of the delivery is the joke itself.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the contrast: a polished TV host saying 'Butthole Surfers' without batting an eye. Economy is near-perfect — the joke costs nothing extra and earns its laugh from the format itself.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: That was very funny. I'm sure you hear that all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, no. Not really.

jokes.text: Backstage, a crew member tries to flirt with a woman by saying 'Wanna come over and watch the show?' — then immediately clarifies 'No, I'm talking to her' when a male colleague responds.
jokes.setup: A crew member makes what sounds like a general invitation backstage.
jokes.punchline: His colleague takes it, forcing the awkward clarification that he was hitting on a woman — undercut by the colleague's oblivious 'OK.'
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional bit of awkward workplace comedy. The misdirection works but the characters are peripheral and the moment is disposable. The oblivious 'OK' from the male colleague is the best part.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: Oh, no. No, no, no, no. I'm from Oklahoma. That's cow country. Someone who still eats red meat.

jokes.text: During the Butthole Surfers' performance, Larry leans over and shouts 'I can't breathe!'
jokes.setup: The Butthole Surfers are performing their chaotic, pyrotechnic set on Larry's talk show.
jokes.punchline: Larry — the anxious, conflict-averse host — is physically undone by his own booking, reduced to gasping.
jokes.explanation: Larry's physical distress during a band performance is a perfect encapsulation of his character — he books transgressive acts for credibility but can't actually handle them. The repeated 'I can't breathe!' escalates the helplessness.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What are you talkin' about? I was kiddin'. You going to call her in?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown crew member
dialogue.line: You bet your ass.

jokes.text: 'No flipping. Butthole Surfers.' — Larry's outro to commercial.
jokes.setup: Larry's standard catchphrase 'No flipping' (don't change the channel) is deployed after an insane, fire-filled performance.
jokes.punchline: Appending 'Butthole Surfers' to the professional catchphrase is both absurd and perfectly banal — he's treating it like any other segment.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical joke. The running-gag catchphrase 'No flipping' is made hilarious by its juxtaposition with 'Butthole Surfers' — the very professionalism of the delivery is the joke. High quotability because of the contrast between the formal TV-host register and the absurd band name.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: 'Butthole' and 'surfing' shouldn't be put together. To me, someone's ass is gonna get waxed, and I don't think that's a good thing.

jokes.text: Larry backstage to the Butthole Surfers: 'What the fuck was that? ... I love fire.' then immediately pivots to 'Let's get together and hang out at a club or something.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just survived a chaotic, apparently fire-featuring performance and confronts the band backstage.
jokes.punchline: His 'I love fire' confession — clearly the opposite of his actual feeling — followed immediately by the hollow social offer of hanging out, reveals Larry's insecure need to seem cool to transgressive artists.
jokes.explanation: This is sharp character comedy. Larry's fundamental insecurity — his need to seem edgier than he is — is laid bare in two lines. The pivot from 'What the fuck was that?' to 'I love fire' is a perfect character contradiction, and the hollow 'let's hang out' seals it. Earns its score through character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Bob Saget says that all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: All the time.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: That's good to know.

jokes.text: Larry asks if the visitor is 'the Korean woman from the commissary' upon hearing the name 'Michelle Hollaway'
jokes.setup: An assistant informs Larry that 'Michelle Hollaway' is here to see him
jokes.punchline: Larry's non-sequitur association of 'hollaway' with 'Korean woman from the commissary' reveals his oblivious, self-absorbed worldview
jokes.explanation: A slightly dated bit of character-specific obliviousness. The assistant's straight-man response ('I don't think Hollaway's a Korean name') is perfectly calibrated. The follow-up 'Don't take that tone with me' is the kicker. Modest but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It's a big fish on, but the thing is Artie gave that to me. It's a whole fishing tackle box/wallet combination.

jokes.text: Hank asks 'Jake Stein my attorney or Jake Stein my accountant?' when a paralegal announces she's from Jake Stein's office.
jokes.setup: A paralegal says she's from 'Jake Stein's office.'
jokes.punchline: Hank has two different Jake Steins — attorney and accountant — revealing the absurdly bloated professional entourage of a minor celebrity.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient joke about Hollywood excess filtered through Hank's character. Having two professionals with the identical name is the right kind of specific absurdity. Works as worldbuilding and character comedy simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah, but the housekeeper's not here, so we'll have to just drink it out of the bottle.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: Straight out of the bottle?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Straight.

jokes.text: Hank, after learning the woman is a paralegal: 'I always thought that was a lawyer in a wheelchair.'
jokes.setup: The paralegal introduces herself as such. Hank affects confusion about the term.
jokes.punchline: His faux-folksy malapropism — parsing 'paralegal' as 'para' (as in paraplegic) + 'legal' — is deliberately stupid, deployed as a flirtatious charm offensive.
jokes.explanation: A classic Hank move: delivering a dumb pun and then soaking in the attention. The paralegal's 'I'm sure you hear that all the time' / 'No, not really' exchange adds a secondary layer — Hank's joke isn't even a known bit, which makes his pride in it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Chocolate is an aphrodisiac, and the mud part is all chocolate.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: Oh, my God.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: I think it's working.

jokes.text: Paralegal: 'I'm sure you hear that all the time.' Hank: 'No, no. Not really.'
jokes.setup: The paralegal politely laughs at Hank's wheelchair joke and assumes it's a stock bit.
jokes.punchline: Hank's sincere denial — he really did just make that up and is genuinely pleased with himself — is funnier than if he'd claimed it was original.
jokes.explanation: The follow-beat is actually better than the joke itself. Hank's genuine pride in a mediocre pun — delivered with Tambor's perfect earnestness — is a distillation of his character. The economy is superb: three words do everything.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: Sitter?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Dog sitter?

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: No, the baby-sitter. Um, I have a 6-year-old son.

jokes.text: Hank asks Michelle if she's a vegetarian and when she says no, calls it 'very refreshing' and invites her to dinner.
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to extend the interaction after a contract signing.
jokes.punchline: His relief that she eats meat — and his framing of a non-vegetarian Oklahoma woman as an exotic novelty in Hollywood — reveals both his loneliness and his Hollywood-bubble worldview.
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat. The joke is in the subtext — Hank is so starved for 'authenticity' that a woman who eats steak is breathtaking. The comedy is quiet and reveals character rather than generating a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, isn't that... isn't that just great?

jokes.text: Hank: 'Oh, no. No, no, no, no. I'm from Oklahoma. That's cow country.' / Hank: 'Someone who still eats red meat. That's very refreshing.'
jokes.setup: Hank asks if Michelle is vegetarian (projecting Hollywood norms onto her)
jokes.punchline: She's from Oklahoma and eats red meat; Hank treats this like an exotic discovery — 'That's very refreshing' — revealing how Hollywood has warped his sense of normalcy
jokes.explanation: A smart observational joke about Hollywood insularity — Hank is so immersed in showbiz culture that a woman from Oklahoma who eats steak is genuinely exotic to him. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: quite frankly, Roger... is that... is that your husband?

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: No, that's my son.

jokes.text: Two crew members rewind a commercial with women on a beach and debate which one is 'the shit,' with one saying 'Come walk to daddy.'
jokes.setup: Two backstage guys are watching TV monitors and get distracted by a commercial.
jokes.punchline: Their escalating objectification — 'the one in the middle is the shit,' 'come walk to daddy,' 'you're naughty' — is so unself-consciously grotesque it becomes its own kind of comedy.
jokes.explanation: The show uses this as a slice-of-life behind-the-scenes snapshot, but the comedy is thin. It's meant to paint the casual sleaziness of the TV world, which it does, but it doesn't rise above that functional purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: Roger... is that your husband?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, that's my son.

jokes.text: One crew member suggests calling the actress's agent 'to hook it up,' then immediately says 'What are you talkin' about? I was kiddin'' — then admits they absolutely are going to call her in.
jokes.setup: A crew member makes what sounds like a half-joke about calling the commercial actress's agent.
jokes.punchline: He denies it's serious for exactly one beat before confirming he's absolutely serious — the fake-out deflation accelerated to immediate honesty.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient beat about the shamelessness of men in the industry. The rapid collapse of the denial is the joke, and it works. Sets up the Phil subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh! I mean, kids are great. They have energy.

jokes.text: 'Butthole' and 'surfing' shouldn't be put together. 'To me, someone's ass is gonna get waxed, and I don't think that's a good thing.'
jokes.setup: Crew members are watching the Butthole Surfers and questioning why they're called a 'surf' band.
jokes.punchline: The character riffs on the band name's two components and arrives at the image of ass-waxing, delivered with earnest conviction.
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing riff on the band name that earns points for committing to the logic of the wordplay through to its uncomfortable conclusion. Not exceptional but playfully executed.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I don't know anyone who has an American car anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: What do you mean? I drive an American car.

jokes.text: 'Bob Saget says that all the time.' / 'Bob? Says... yeah.' / 'All the time. That's good to know.'
jokes.setup: Someone says 'you don't want to get your ass waxed' and the other attributes this as a frequent Bob Saget saying.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Bob Saget — America's Full House dad — says 'you don't want to get your ass waxed' all the time is a perfect celebrity-subversion joke. 'That's good to know' is the ideal underplayed response.
jokes.explanation: A lovely quick joke that anticipates the real Bob Saget's famously raunchy off-screen persona (this is 1997 Full House era). The deadpan 'that's good to know' is the perfect button. Good economy, good subversion of celebrity image.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It's a hell of a lot better than these rice burners and strudel wagons the rest of these assholes in Hollywood drive.

jokes.text: Hank shows Michelle his wallet: 'Artie gave that to me. It's a whole fishing tackle box/wallet combination.'
jokes.setup: Michelle notices Hank's unusual wallet with a fish on it during their dinner.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that it's a fishing tackle box/wallet hybrid — a gift from gruff producer Artie — is absurdly specific and reveals the odd tenderness of their relationship.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful piece of character worldbuilding. The fishing tackle box/wallet is exactly absurd enough to be funny, and the fact that it's a gift from Artie adds warmth to an otherwise gruff character. The specificity is what elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, what about little Miguelito from Peru? You know, the kid that you adopted through Sally Struthers? All his letters pile up like goddamned junk mail.

jokes.text: Hank: 'The housekeeper's not here, so we'll have to just drink it out of the bottle.' Michelle: 'Straight out of the bottle?' Hank: 'Straight.'
jokes.setup: Hank offers more wine at his home, then realizes the housekeeper isn't there to manage serving.
jokes.punchline: His complete dependence on domestic help — to the point where wine-pouring is beyond him — is delivered with total unselfconsciousness. 'Straight' as a one-word button is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Economy is the star here. 'Straight.' as a one-word punchline after the revelation of Hank's domestic helplessness is perfectly timed. The joke is about his childlike dependence on staff, delivered without self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, what am I supposed to do? He wrote them in Spanish.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Chocolate is an aphrodisiac, and the mud part is all chocolate.'
jokes.setup: Hank encourages Michelle to try the mud pie dessert during their date.
jokes.punchline: His clumsy attempt to make dessert-eating erotic by explaining that mud pie is chocolate and chocolate is an aphrodisiac — delivered with complete earnestness — is perfectly Hank.
jokes.explanation: The seduction logic is beautifully flawed: he's explaining the 'mud' in mud pie as a selling point for romance. Tambor's delivery makes this — the kind of thing only Hank would say with utter sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Showfolk belong with showfolk, Hank. If you're not careful, you're gonna mess this kid up and his mom.

jokes.text: Michelle eats the mud pie and says 'Oh, my God.' Hank asks 'What?' She says 'I think it's working.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just explained that chocolate is an aphrodisiac.
jokes.punchline: Michelle immediately reports that it's 'working' — playing along with his absurd logic in a way that rewards his earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Good callback/payoff to the aphrodisiac setup. The joke is clean and quick. Michelle's participation in Hank's seduction logic — genuinely or ironically — makes the moment warm and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Mama Lucia. Fabuloosa caboosa. Great ass, too.

jokes.text: Date is going well, chemistry is building — then Michelle says she has to call 'the sitter.' Hank: 'Sitter? Dog sitter?' She reveals she has a 6-year-old son.
jokes.setup: The date is clearly going in a romantic direction.
jokes.punchline: Hank's optimistic 'Dog sitter?' — hoping for the least complicated answer — before learning she has a child is a perfect beat of comic desperation.
jokes.explanation: Hank's 'Dog sitter?' is a beautifully economical expression of wishful thinking. He's mentally hoping this is the most benign possible version of the news. The beat is character-specific and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Oh, that's because Phil doesn't have an office.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Well, isn't that... isn't that just great?' — learning to hide his disappointment about the child while continuing to pursue Michelle.
jokes.setup: Michelle has revealed she has a 6-year-old son. Hank must recalibrate his romantic intentions in real time.
jokes.punchline: His stilted, over-the-top enthusiasm ('isn't that just great?') is transparently manufactured, and the comedy is in watching Tambor work through the recalculation.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy. The hesitation and forced enthusiasm are Tambor's domain. Not a huge laugh but a rich character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: 20 bucks? I hope it's a day of beauty.

jokes.text: Michelle: 'A lot of men lose interest after they hear that [she has a kid].' Hank: 'I mean... well, quite frankly... is that your husband?' — referring to the son's name Roger.
jokes.setup: Michelle explains that men lose interest when they learn she has a son named Roger.
jokes.punchline: Hank's moment of confusion — asking if 'Roger' is her husband — reveals he momentarily panicked about a different complication entirely.
jokes.explanation: A good beat. Hank's instant pivot to 'is that your husband?' shows his anxiety about romantic competition even amid his current anxiety about the child. Efficient multi-layer character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: My money's missing.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Gosh, Larry. If you don't wanna buy one, just say so.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, I believe you. My money's gone.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Oh! I mean, kids are great. They have energy.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to convince Michelle he loves kids after initially panicking.
jokes.punchline: 'They have energy' as the only endorsement of children Hank can summon reveals his total unfamiliarity with them.
jokes.explanation: The hollow universality of 'they have energy' is perfect — it's the thing you say when you know nothing positive to say about children specifically. Economy is strong; the pause before 'They have energy' is doing heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: It's more like a concept at this point.

jokes.text: Hank to Artie: 'She lives in Chatsworth. And they have one car. It's American. I don't know anyone who has an American car anymore.'
jokes.setup: Hank is reporting back to Artie about Michelle's admirable ordinariness.
jokes.punchline: His astonishment that someone owns an American car — treated as exotica — perfectly captures Hollywood bubble insularity.
jokes.explanation: Good observational comedy about the Hollywood bubble. The escalating checklist of her 'realness' (Chatsworth, one car, American) works as a comedic sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Keith
dialogue.line: Oh, come on. Have a cookie.

dialogue.speaker: Actress
dialogue.line: So there's nothing for me to read?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: You want something to read? We got papers here. We got everything.

jokes.text: Artie: 'It's a hell of a lot better than these rice burners and strudel wagons the rest of these assholes in Hollywood drive.'
jokes.setup: Hank is surprised anyone drives an American car; Artie reveals he does.
jokes.punchline: Artie's casual use of dated ethnic slurs for Japanese and German cars ('rice burners and strudel wagons') — delivered with the certainty of a man who has never been questioned — is a perfect Rip Torn character moment.
jokes.explanation: 'Strudel wagons' is the standout coinage here — it's a completely invented slur that's more absurd than offensive, and the pairing with 'rice burners' reveals Artie as a man from a different era who has simply never updated his vocabulary. Rip Torn is the only person who could deliver this with the right mixture of righteousness and obliviousness. High character integration score because this is quintessentially Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Listen, you gotta be very careful when you accuse a friend of stealing money because many years ago, I was in New York with Lenny Bruce, and, uh, he accused me of taking 50 bucks from him, and it turned very ugly and I popped him.

jokes.text: Hank: 'And what about little miguelito from Peru? You know, the kid that you adopted through Sally Struthers? All his letters pile up like goddamned junk mail.' Hank: 'Well, what am I supposed to do? He wrote them in Spanish.'
jokes.setup: Artie warns Hank against getting involved with a 'real' woman and her child, noting Hank's pattern of neglecting commitments.
jokes.punchline: Hank's defense of ignoring his sponsored Peruvian child is that the child wrote to him in Spanish — an absurd abdication of responsibility delivered without shame.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. The setup — that Hank adopted a Peruvian child through Sally Struthers (a perfect '90s cultural reference) and simply ignores the letters — is already dark and funny. But the punchline — 'He wrote them in Spanish' — is a masterclass in character-specific comic logic. Hank isn't a monster, just profoundly self-absorbed and entitled. The excuse is so perfectly insufficient that it earns the escalating absurdity. This is the kind of joke that defines a character for seasons. Comparable in quality to the anchor examples provided.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You know, you've told me this story before, and, uh, you took the money.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That may be, but I'm just trying to warn you.

jokes.text: Hank: 'This is not gonna happen with Roger, because he's local.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just called out Hank's neglect of his sponsored Peruvian child.
jokes.punchline: Hank's solution to the geographic/language barrier problem with Miguelito is to simply pursue a local child — as if proximity alone solves his character defects.
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback button to the Miguelito joke. Hank's logic — that the problem with the Peruvian boy was logistics, not his own neglect — is both darkly funny and devastating as character revelation. The economy is superb: five words ('because he's local') do enormous work. Earns its high score through specificity and the way it deepens the prior joke.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: I know we're early, it's just they were so speedy over there at Midas Muffler.

jokes.text: A woman walks by and Artie mutters 'Whoa. Whoa. Mama lucia. Fabuloosa caboosa. Great ass, too.'
jokes.setup: Artie is in the middle of giving Hank serious life advice.
jokes.punchline: Artie instantly abandons his sage mentor posture to ogle a passing woman with pseudo-Spanish appreciations, then seamlessly asks 'Can you help me?' as if nothing happened.
jokes.explanation: Artie's hypocrisy — lecturing Hank on professionalism while immediately objectifying a passing woman — is perfectly Rip Torn. 'Fabuloosa caboosa' is a good coinage. The transition to 'Can you help me?' is a great deadpan reset.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Uh-oh, you must be Susan. You must be Roger. How you doin', champ?

dialogue.speaker: Roger
dialogue.line: Fine. They took my mom's car and lifted it way high.

jokes.text: Beverly: 'You don't see me setting up fake meetings just to meet Ed Asner.'
jokes.setup: Beverly is calling Phil out for his fake casting scheme.
jokes.punchline: Her specific counter-example — that she doesn't arrange fake meetings to meet Ed Asner — is the joke. The specificity of Ed Asner as Beverly's aspirational celebrity crush is unexpected and perfect.
jokes.explanation: Ed Asner is the perfect choice — an older, gruff character actor who wouldn't be anyone's obvious celebrity crush. The specificity elevates what could be a generic line into a genuine character joke. Beverly's deadpan delivery of her own hypothetical sleaziness is also self-aware and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Sacramento... that's the capital of California. Wow. You are correct.

dialogue.speaker: Roger
dialogue.line: You must... you must be very smart.

jokes.text: Phil: 'Beverly, kiss my ass.' Beverly: 'You show it bare.'
jokes.setup: Phil, cornered, tells Beverly to kiss his ass.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's one-beat return — 'You show it bare' — is an aggressive, deadpan escalation that catches Phil (and the audience) off guard.
jokes.explanation: Beverly's comeback is quick, unexpected, and perfectly deadpan. 'You show it bare' implies she's not only willing but setting conditions — a great inversion. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: South Dakota. Pierre. And what's the capital of North Dakota... Pepé Le Pew?

jokes.text: Phil asks the actress how she got her job — 'You go in there and you have to wear a bathing suit?' She confirms. Phil: 'That's how I got this job. Honestly. You know what's odd is I wear a 2-piece.'
jokes.setup: Phil is pretending to commiserate with an actress about the objectification in the industry.
jokes.punchline: Phil pivots to claiming he also got his job by wearing a bathing suit — specifically a 2-piece — which is both absurdist and a weirdly effective self-deprecating confession of his own sleaziness.
jokes.explanation: The '2-piece' detail is the joke's engine — it's so specific and unexpected that it earns a real laugh. Phil's attempt to bond with the actress via shared objectification while being the objectifier is darkly comic.

dialogue.speaker: Roger
dialogue.line: You're funny, Mr. Kingsley.

jokes.text: Larry: asked about a raffle ticket, says 'Oh, sure. How much is it?' / 'Twenty bucks.' / 'Twenty bucks? I hope it's a day of beauty.'
jokes.setup: Beverly asks Larry to buy a raffle ticket for her niece's school; he asks the price
jokes.punchline: 'Twenty bucks? I hope it's a day of beauty' — a backhanded insult suggesting the $20 prize should at minimum be something cosmetic
jokes.explanation: A quick, tight joke — Larry's cheapness and mild vanity wrapped into one. 'Day of beauty' is a slightly dated but perfectly specific choice. Economical.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Those are beautiful earrings.

dialogue.speaker: Lori
dialogue.line: Oh, thanks. I got 'em today.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, really?

dialogue.speaker: Lori
dialogue.line: Yeah. I used the money I got from, uh... my wallet?

jokes.text: Larry complains about money missing from his wallet after the raffle ticket setup, leading to Beverly thinking he just doesn't want to buy a ticket.
jokes.setup: Beverly asks Larry to buy a raffle ticket for her niece's school. He balks at the $20 price, says 'My money's missing.'
jokes.punchline: Beverly's flat 'Gosh, Larry. If you don't wanna buy one, just say so' — assuming he's making up the missing money as a cheap excuse — is a perfect beat. The audience knows he's actually paranoid about Lori, adding irony.
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — the audience has information Beverly doesn't, creating dramatic irony. Larry's real paranoia reads as petty cheapness to Beverly, which is a double indictment of his character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You know what? I always give them a couple hundred bucks because you know what? You know, they know me.

jokes.text: Larry: '20 bucks? I hope it's a day of beauty.'
jokes.setup: Beverly asks Larry to buy a $20 raffle ticket for her niece's school.
jokes.punchline: Larry's response — hoping the prize is 'a day of beauty' — is a perfectly petty, self-absorbed reaction that reveals his character while getting a laugh.
jokes.explanation: Larry's idea of 'a day of beauty' as worth $20 is a good little character joke — vain, LA-centric, and delivered with perfect economy. The specific choice of 'day of beauty' over any other prize is character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That bird was supposed to shit on Larry's hand.

jokes.text: Keith barges into Phil's meeting with the actress carrying cookies and beverages, trying to ingratiate himself.
jokes.setup: Phil is conducting his fake casting meeting with an actress when Keith arrives uninvited.
jokes.punchline: Keith's transparently desperate attempt to insert himself — 'our lovely guest might like a delightful beverage or one of these equally-delightful cookies' — while Phil tries to eject him.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy about workplace sleaziness doubling up. The 'delightful' repeated twice is a nice touch of over-selling. Not exceptional but works as escalation of the Phil subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Come on. Reba McEntire doesn't need to do 2 songs. Some guy left her, and she's broke. Big fucking deal. We got it the first time.

jokes.text: Phil: 'You want something to read? We got papers here. We got everything.' — desperately overcovering when the actress asks for a script
jokes.setup: The actress asks if there's anything to read — expecting an actual script for the meeting she was called in for
jokes.punchline: Phil, who has no script because this was a fake booking, gestures frantically at random papers: 'We got papers here. We got everything.'
jokes.explanation: Phil's panicked improvisation is a good cringe-comedy beat. 'We got papers here. We got everything' is funny precisely because it's such a nothing answer — papers — as if volume covers for content.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: You don't see me setting up fake meetings just to meet Ed Asner.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Many years ago I was in New York with Lenny Bruce, and he accused me of taking 50 bucks from him, and it turned very ugly and I popped him.' Larry: 'You've told me this story before, and you took the money.' Artie: 'That may be, but I'm just trying to warn you.'
jokes.setup: Artie begins a cautionary tale about accusing a friend of theft, using Lenny Bruce as his example.
jokes.punchline: Larry reveals Artie took the money from Lenny Bruce. Artie's non-denial — 'That may be' — while continuing to present himself as the moral authority of the anecdote is perfect.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent. The three-beat structure is perfectly executed: (1) Artie sets up a moral tale, (2) Larry reveals Artie was the thief, (3) Artie acknowledges this with 'That may be' and proceeds to give the advice anyway. The 'That may be' is one of the best non-denial denials in the episode. The Lenny Bruce name-drop grounds it historically while being characteristically Artie. High character integration — only Artie would punch Lenny Bruce, steal from him, and still use the story as a cautionary tale for others.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Beverly, kiss my ass.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: You show it bare.

jokes.text: Artie's Lenny Bruce story: 'Many years ago I was in New York with Lenny Bruce, and he accused me of taking $50 from him, and it turned very ugly and I popped him.'
jokes.setup: Artie is warning Hank to be careful about accusing Lori of theft
jokes.punchline: His cautionary tale involves having punched Lenny Bruce — which is not the usual lesson one draws from such a story
jokes.explanation: Artie is one of the great TV characters, and moments like this are why: he casually drops that he punched Lenny Bruce as if it's a normal anecdote, and it lands perfectly. The show's universe is exactly the kind of place where Artie would have been in the room with Lenny Bruce. Strong character integration — nobody else could tell this story.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: They're not horses, Phil.

jokes.text: Artie: 'You better keep your guard up, because Lori's going to pop you.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just admitted he punched Lenny Bruce (while being the actual thief).
jokes.punchline: Artie warns Larry that if he accuses Lori of theft, she'll punch him — completing the parallel, but now the 'popping' is presented as the outcome for the accuser, not the thief.
jokes.explanation: A good button to the Lenny Bruce story. The irony that Artie — the actual thief who punched the person he'd robbed — is now warning Larry about being punched is efficiently delivered. The word 'pop' carrying over from the story is a nice structural echo.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: This sort of thing happens in the movies, maybe, but we had no idea this sort of behavior was being conducted on the very premises of the Larry Sanders show.

jokes.text: Larry notices 'love' written on his headshots and demands to know who did it. The answer: Beverly, 'for the affiliates.'
jokes.setup: Larry is already paranoid and agitated when he sees 'love' inscribed on his headshots.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's completely reasonable explanation — it's standard for affiliate mailings — makes Larry's outrage ('Who the fuck wrote that?!') seem like comic overreaction.
jokes.explanation: A functional Larry-paranoia beat. His horror at 'love' being written in his name — without context — is characteristically self-absorbed. The joke is mild but character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Shut the fuck up, Phil!

jokes.text: Hank to Roger (6-year-old): 'Sacramento... that's the capital of California.' Roger: 'Wow.'
jokes.setup: Roger has just correctly identified Pierre as the capital of South Dakota. Hank offers that Sacramento is the capital of California.
jokes.punchline: Roger's 'Wow' — the same impressed response he's been giving to genuinely difficult geography answers — applied to the most well-known state capital is a perfect reversal. The child is humoring the adult.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical beat. Hank — a grown adult on a TV show — feels compelled to contribute to the geography game and picks the easiest possible capital. Roger's 'Wow' (the child politely matching energy) is the joke. The role reversal — child indulging adult — is sweet and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Actress
dialogue.line: You know what's odd is I wear a 2-piece.

jokes.text: Hank: 'And what's the capital of north dakota... Pepé le Peu?' — testing Roger with a fake punchline answer.
jokes.setup: Hank is playing the geography capitals game with young Roger.
jokes.punchline: After Roger correctly identifies Pierre (capital of South Dakota), Hank asks about North Dakota and offers 'Pepé le Peu' as if it's a hint — a non-sequitur cartoon character standing in for a geography answer.
jokes.explanation: Hank's attempt at a joke for a child — conflating 'Bismarck' with Pepé le Peu — is the kind of thing a desperate-to-be-liked adult does. The joke works because of what it reveals about Hank rather than being clever in itself.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Something seems... Reba... she was anxious to get on the road. There was a big turquoise and silver fair in Santa Fe tomorrow.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I think I really like you.' — said to Roger the 6-year-old, mirroring what Susan said about Roger liking Hank
jokes.setup: Susan says 'I think he really likes you'
jokes.punchline: Hank responds to Roger directly: 'Well, that's a coincidence, 'cause I think I really like you' — treating a 6-year-old like a mutual crush
jokes.explanation: Sweet and slightly absurd — Hank applying adult social pleasantries to a 6-year-old is a consistent comic register throughout this subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Something seems... Reba... she was anxious to get on the road. There was a big turquoise and silver fair in Santa Fe tomorrow.

jokes.text: Hank invites Roger on the show to play the geography game. Roger agrees. Hank: 'Oh! Ow!' — apparently hurting himself in excitement.
jokes.setup: Hank is overexcited about Roger's agreement to appear on the show.
jokes.punchline: Hank's exuberant 'Super-duper!' celebration physically injures him — his enthusiasm literally exceeds his physical limitations.
jokes.explanation: A quick physical comedy beat. Hank's self-injury from his own enthusiasm is a light gag — functional but not memorable. Works best as punctuation to the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Come on. You know this. He knew all the capitals of all the states. Backstage he was terrific. Come on. Starts with an 'I.' Ends with a 'y.'

jokes.text: Lori Loughlin stops by the set. Larry notices her new earrings, she says she got them today. Larry: 'Did you get them with... my wallet?'
jokes.setup: Lori visits and Larry notices her new earrings, which she acquired on the day money went missing from his wallet.
jokes.punchline: Larry's transition from compliment to accusation — stopping himself mid-sentence — is a perfect cringe beat. His inability to let it go despite the social awkwardness is pure Larry.
jokes.explanation: The structural execution is excellent — Larry leads with a genuine compliment, she volunteers the timing ('I got them today'), and his response almost forms the question before catching itself. The pause before 'my wallet?' is a perfect cringe beat. Genuinely uncomfortable in the best Larry Sanders way.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Don't touch the boy.

jokes.text: Lori: 'I probably overtipped the parking valet. That's it. You know what? I always give them a couple hundred bucks because you know what? You know, they know me.'
jokes.setup: Lori is deflecting Larry's implicit accusation about the missing money.
jokes.punchline: Her increasingly elaborate explanation — she routinely gives parking valets $200 because 'they know her' — is both a transparent lie and an accidentally funny portrait of celebrity narcissism.
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of Lori's alibi — parking valets getting $200 because they know her — works as both character comedy and cringe. The specificity of the dollar amount makes it funnier.

dialogue.line: Nice booking. The kid froze.

jokes.text: Artie about Hank booking Roger: 'Does he know where your head is? Because I think it's up your ass.'
jokes.setup: Hank defends booking Roger, a 6-year-old geography whiz, on the show without authorization.
jokes.punchline: Artie pivots the geography framing — 'does he know where things are?' — into an anatomical insult, specifically 'your head is up your ass.'
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed geography/anatomy pun from Artie. The setup (geography whiz) gives him the ammunition for the wordplay, and it lands cleanly. This is the kind of thing Rip Torn does effortlessly.

dialogue.speaker: Michelle
dialogue.line: You are a grown man, you had no reason to attack him like that. He did great. It went great.

jokes.text: Artie on the mynah bird that was supposed to sing show tunes: 'That bird was supposed to shit on Larry's hand.'
jokes.setup: Hank defends booking Roger by saying he's better than the mynah bird that 'just shit on Larry's hand'
jokes.punchline: Artie's correction: 'That bird was supposed to shit on Larry's hand' — meaning it was a planned bit that Larry agreed to
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's great jokes. The mynah bird bit reveals the absurdist world of late-night television — Larry agreed to have a bird defecate on his hand as entertainment. Artie's calm correction ('was supposed to shit on his hand') implies this was a planned, professional booking decision. The economy is perfect. Deeply quotable. Strong character integration — only Artie would make this distinction.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You know, I've seen kids with Michael Jackson less nervous.

jokes.text: Artie: 'That bird was supposed to shit on Larry's hand.'
jokes.setup: Hank defends his booking by comparing it favorably to a previous bad booking — a mynah bird that was supposed to sing show tunes.
jokes.punchline: Artie's correction — the bird was indeed supposed to shit on Larry's hand, that was the INTENT, not a failure — reframes the prior bit as deliberately transgressive rather than accidentally gross.
jokes.explanation: This is a gem. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) Artie casually reveals that bird-defecation-on-Larry was a deliberate production choice, (2) this retroactively damns Artie's own taste in bookings while he criticizes Hank's, (3) the deadpan certainty of 'that bird was SUPPOSED to shit on Larry's hand' is perfect Rip Torn delivery. High economy, high character integration, and genuinely surprising. Earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Just remember, this show is not about you getting laid. It's about Larry getting laid.

jokes.text: Artie to Hank: 'You got one fucking segment, Hank. That's it.' Hank: 'All right.' Artie immediately turns to food table: 'Take as much as you want, ladies. There's plenty more.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just delivered a stern edict to Hank about the booking.
jokes.punchline: Artie's instant tonal whiplash — from hard-nosed producer to gracious food-table host — is perfectly Rip Torn. The juxtaposition of the two modes in two seconds is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The tonal pivot is the joke. Artie moves from 'one fucking segment, that's it' to 'take as much as you want, ladies' in a single breath. It's pure Rip Torn character comedy — the man contains multitudes and switches between them without transition.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Listen, I... I don't know how to tell you how sorry I am about that, because I just thought that she took the money...

dialogue.speaker: John Stamos
dialogue.line: No, no, no. No, you misunderstood. Um, I came down here because... well, she did take the money.

jokes.text: Jennette's agent shows up demanding a script for the 'meeting' that Phil invented. Beverly: 'Boggles the mind, Mr. Rindels.'
jokes.setup: An agent has arrived to follow up on Phil's fake casting meeting, demanding a script.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's performative outrage — 'Boggles the mind, Mr. Rindels. This sort of thing happens in the movies, maybe, but we had no idea this sort of behavior was being conducted on the very premises of the Larry Sanders show' — delivered while Phil is standing right there.
jokes.explanation: Beverly's fake-outrage performance for the agent — over-the-top institutional indignation on behalf of a show that absolutely tolerates this — is good industry satire. The formal diction ('on the very premises') adds comedic weight.

dialogue.speaker: John Stamos
dialogue.line: No, you misunderstood. Um, I came down here because... well, she did take the money.

jokes.text: Phil shouts 'Shut the fuck up, Phil!' — catching himself, or directed at himself in frustration, while trying to manage the agent situation.
jokes.setup: Beverly is performatively selling out Phil to the agent while Phil tries to manage the situation.
jokes.punchline: Phil tells Beverly to shut up but uses his own name — either confusion under pressure or self-directed frustration — a brief, odd moment.
jokes.explanation: A quick comedic stumble. Phil saying 'shut the fuck up, Phil' in what appears to be a moment of self-directed frustration is mildly funny but not well-developed.

dialogue.speaker: John Stamos
dialogue.line: I know, it's weird. It's... she's, uh... she's had this problem for a while now really? Yeah, and she was embarrassed and she wanted me to bring the money down here, because she didn't, you know... you know, I mean, you could imagine how it...

jokes.text: Artie explains why Reba didn't do a second song: 'There was a big turquoise and silver fair in Santa Fe tomorrow.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks why Reba McEntire left early instead of doing the show.
jokes.punchline: Artie's completely specific, completely absurd explanation — a 'turquoise and silver fair in Santa Fe' — as a celebrity's priority over TV performance is a perfect non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'turquoise and silver fair in Santa Fe' is what makes this funny — it's exactly the kind of thing Reba McEntire might actually prioritize. Artie delivers it as if it's a completely satisfactory answer, which is the joke. The absurd specificity elevates it above generic celebrity-diva material.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: There was 250 in the wallet. There's 200 here. Is that a new earring?

jokes.text: Roger, the supposed geography prodigy, is brought on stage and freezes completely, unable to identify Italy ('Starts with an I, ends with a Y, looks like a boot').
jokes.setup: Hank has booked 6-year-old Roger as a geography expert. On stage, Larry gives the easiest possible geography question — Italy, famously boot-shaped.
jokes.punchline: Roger completely freezes, saying nothing. The more hints Larry and Hank give, the more absolute the silence. The prodigy is simply a normal 6-year-old who was good at a game at a dinner table.
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed payoff to the Hank-Roger subplot. The comedy is earned through escalation: the more helpfully specific the hints ('starts with an I, ends with a Y, looks like a boot'), the more devastating the silence. It's a perfect cringe set piece about the gap between private performance and public pressure. The callback to the dinner-table geography game makes this land harder.

jokes.text: Roger freezes completely on the first question — Italy, shaped like a boot, starts with I, ends with Y — and cannot answer
jokes.setup: Roger has been established as a geography whiz who nails every state capital; he's been brought on national TV to demonstrate this
jokes.punchline: He completely freezes on Italy — one of the most recognizable countries in the world — even with Larry providing the shape, the starting letter, and the ending letter
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the episode's central comic setup. Everything since Roger's introduction has been building to this moment of total failure. The structure is near-perfect: establish the ability with excessive specificity (state capitals!), raise the stakes (national TV), make the question trivially easy (Italy!), provide escalating hints, and have the child say nothing. Larry's desperate hint-giving makes it worse. The impact is high because it's fully earned — we invested in this disaster.

jokes.text: Larry's on-air desperation: 'Come on. You know this. He knew all the capitals of all the states. Backstage he was terrific. Come on.' / 'Starts with an I. Ends with a Y.'
jokes.setup: Roger has frozen; Larry is trying to salvage the segment live on air
jokes.punchline: Larry's increasingly desperate, increasingly infantilizing hints — 'Starts with an I. Ends with a Y.' — reveal his professional panic while making the situation worse
jokes.explanation: Larry's talk-show professionalism in full collapse is one of the show's great recurring veins of comedy. 'Backstage he was terrific' is the most desperate thing a host can say live on air — it confirms the disaster while trying to reassign blame. The escalating hints get funnier as they become more obviously futile.

jokes.text: Larry to Hank, during Roger's on-air freeze: 'Don't snap at him. He's not... you just gotta look... you're not looking at the map.' Artie off-camera: 'Oh, jeez. Nice booking.'
jokes.setup: Roger has frozen on stage and Larry and Hank are desperately trying to prompt him.
jokes.punchline: Artie's off-camera deadpan verdict — 'Nice booking' — during the public disaster is the perfect Greek chorus comment. The chaos of two adults panicking over a silent child is punctuated by Artie's absolute calm.
jokes.explanation: 'Nice booking' in two words delivers Artie's entire editorial position on the situation. The economy is superb. As a reaction beat to the chaos, it's perfectly timed and characteristically dry.

jokes.text: Artie's backhanded reaction from the control booth: 'Oh, jeez. Nice booking.'
jokes.setup: The Roger segment is a disaster unfolding on live TV
jokes.punchline: Artie watches from the booth and offers 'Oh, jeez. Nice booking.' — maximum withering understatement
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'Nice booking' is a perfect ironic callback — he predicted this, he gave Hank one segment anyway, and now he watches it collapse. The economy is exceptional. 'Oh, jeez' as the windup is perfectly calibrated. Strong character integration — this is exactly what Artie would say.

jokes.text: Susan to Hank: 'You are a grown man, you had no reason to attack him like that.' Hank: 'He did great. It went great.'
jokes.setup: After the on-air disaster, Susan confronts Hank about putting her son on television.
jokes.punchline: Hank's flat denial of what just happened — 'He did great. It went great.' — in the face of obvious disaster is a perfect character beat.
jokes.explanation: Hank's reality-denial is a good character moment. 'He did great. It went great.' delivered with conviction after what we've just witnessed is a small, clean joke about self-delusion.

jokes.text: Artie to Hank: 'You know, I've seen kids with Michael Jackson less nervous.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to defend Roger's disastrous on-air appearance.
jokes.punchline: Artie's casual Michael Jackson reference — implying Roger should have been MORE at ease than kids in that particular context — is a darkly transgressive celebrity joke delivered with perfect Artie nonchalance.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely transgressive joke that still lands because of its perfect economy and the character-specific delivery. Artie — who doesn't moralize — drops a Michael Jackson reference that implies something dark about 'kids with Michael Jackson' with absolute calm. In 1997, this was a brave topical joke. The compression is remarkable: nine words carry an enormous amount of subversive comedy. High character integration — only Artie says this, only Artie doesn't flinch after saying it.

jokes.text: Artie: 'You know, I've seen kids with Michael Jackson less nervous.'
jokes.setup: Artie is debriefing the disaster with Hank
jokes.punchline: Artie compares Roger's nervousness unfavorably to children appearing with Michael Jackson — a deeply dark joke about what it implies regarding Michael Jackson and children
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and darkest jokes. The Michael Jackson reference would have been timely and edgy at this point in the show's run (mid-90s, post-first accusation). Artie using it as a benchmark for child comfort levels is both shocking and precisely calibrated — it's not a ham-fisted reference but a genuinely twisted comparison that works on multiple levels. Exceptional character integration: only Artie would say this. Economy is near-perfect. This is a joke that would make a room of comedy writers applaud.

jokes.text: Artie to Hank: 'Just remember, this show is not about you getting laid. It's about Larry getting laid.'
jokes.setup: Artie is concluding his lecture to Hank about misusing the show's resources for personal romantic pursuits.
jokes.punchline: His final verdict is not 'don't use the show for sex' but 'use the show for Larry's sex' — a statement that is simultaneously a joke about celebrity hierarchy and a genuine production philosophy.
jokes.explanation: This is the best line in the episode. 'This show is not about you getting laid. It's about Larry getting laid.' earns its high score on every dimension: (1) Originality — the inversion from moral prohibition to hierarchical correction is completely unexpected, (2) Structure — the two-sentence rhythm is perfect, (3) Character Integration — only Artie, who is simultaneously the show's moral anchor and its most cynical operator, can deliver this as both a joke and a genuine institutional principle, (4) Economy — no wasted words, (5) Earned — it's not cheap transgression, it emerges organically from the Hank storyline. Comparable in quality to the provided anchor examples. This line captures the entire ethos of The Larry Sanders Show in 15 words.

jokes.text: John Stamos arrives to apologize on behalf of Lori Loughlin — and confirms she actually did steal the money.
jokes.setup: Larry believes Lori stole from him. John Stamos arrives and Larry expects an apology for the accusation.
jokes.punchline: John confirms she stole it — validating Larry's paranoia entirely — subverting the expected 'you were wrong to suspect her' resolution.
jokes.explanation: The structural subversion here is excellent. The show builds the entire episode around Larry's paranoid suspicion of Lori, setting up the audience to expect him to be wrong (classic cringe setup). Instead, he was right. The confirmation from John Stamos — a real celebrity, treating Lori's kleptomania as an established fact — is a great dark comedy reveal.

jokes.text: John returns $200 of the $250 stolen. Larry: 'There was 250 in the wallet. There's 200 here.' Long pause. John: 'Is that a new earring?'
jokes.setup: John has returned money on behalf of the kleptomaniac Lori Loughlin. Larry counts it and notes $50 is missing.
jokes.punchline: John's pivot to 'Is that a new earring?' — immediately redirecting to avoid accounting for the missing $50 — implies John may have kept some. It's a perfect callback to the earring earlier in the scene (Lori's new earrings bought with stolen money) and suggests the corruption runs deeper.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best structural joke and the perfect button. Multiple layers working simultaneously: (1) The $50 discrepancy is noticed — John has clearly kept a finder's fee for himself, (2) 'Is that a new earring?' is a direct callback to the exact detail (new earrings) that triggered Larry's suspicion of Lori earlier in the episode, (3) The implication is that JOHN has now also stolen $50, extending the theft one more level, (4) The pivot is the exact same social-deflection move Lori used, suggesting John learned it from her or it's simply how their circle operates. This is a masterclass in episode-length joke construction — every beat of the episode converges in this single question. Economy is near-perfect. Earns 9+ because it's a legitimate television-comedy standout moment.

tmdb_overview: Larry becomes convinced that his new paramour Lori Loughlin has taken money from his wallet. Hank tries to impress a woman by putting her precocious son on the show as an expert in geography. Phil arranges for phony auditions so he can meet some beautiful actresses.
